lesson.title: The Network Layer: Getting a Packet Across Networks, Not Just Across One
lesson.summary: The network layer provides logical addressing and routing so data can travel across many interconnected networks rather than just one local segment, the job performed chiefly by IP.
lesson.body:
The data link layer, as the previous chapter explained, is very good at delivering a frame to the correct device within a single local network segment, but it has no concept of anything beyond that segment. A MAC address cannot tell a switch how to send data to a computer on a completely different network in another city. The network layer, Layer 3 in the OSI model and the Internet layer in the TCP IP model, exists specifically to solve this bigger problem: getting data from a source on one network to a destination on a possibly very distant, different network, potentially crossing many networks in between.

The primary protocol at this layer on the Internet is IP, the Internet Protocol, and its core tool for solving the problem is logical addressing combined with routing. Every device connected to the Internet is assigned an IP address, a number that, unlike a MAC address, is organized hierarchically so that large blocks of addresses can be grouped by network. Devices called routers sit at the boundaries between networks, and each one examines the destination IP address in a packet's header and forwards that packet toward the next router, one hop closer to its destination, without needing to know the complete path in advance.

A worked example shows why this matters. Suppose a student in Minnesota sends data to a server in another state. The data link layer can only get that data as far as the student's own local network and its immediate router, since MAC addressing simply does not extend any further. From there, the network layer takes over: the packet's IP header, added through encapsulation as described earlier, carries the destination IP address, and each router along the path reads that address, consults its own routing information, and forwards the packet to the next router, repeating this process across possibly a dozen or more hops until the packet reaches the destination network and finally the destination device. At no point does any single router need to know the entire route, each one only needs to know which direction is closer to the destination.

This is the essential difference between the data link layer and the network layer, and it is worth stating plainly. The data link layer's MAC addressing and frames operate within one local segment and get replaced fresh at every hop, a new frame with new MAC addresses is built each time a packet crosses from one local network to the next. The network layer's IP addressing and packet header, by contrast, stay the same, unchanged from source to destination across the entire journey, which is exactly what allows routers along the way to keep forwarding it correctly toward the same ultimate target.

Together, these two layers illustrate the payoff of layered architecture in the most concrete way possible. The physical layer moves bits, the data link layer moves frames one local hop at a time, and the network layer, building on both, moves a packet across an entire internetwork of many local segments, each layer relying on the one below it while solving a problem the one below it fundamentally cannot.
